claims.text: HEAs contain at least five principal elements.
The proposed particles are 5–100 nm in size.
The proposed particles are near-equiatomic.
HEA nanoparticles can be supported on substrates.
The relevant substrates are inert.
The particles have a nominally solid structure at room temperature.
Surface segregation and local disorder drive premelting in HEA nanoparticles.
Surface rearrangements establish a transient liquid-like outer shell below the bulk melting temperature.
Lower-melting-point or surface-active elements preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle shell.
Shell segregation facilitates surface melting before melting of the bulk core.
Local disorder and differential bonding among the constituent elements promote formation of a disordered surface region at elevated temperature.
The disordered surface region reduces the energy required for partial melting.
Engineered surface segregation lowers the effective premelting temperature relative to a composition without engineered segregation.
Surface-enriched nanoparticles should show earlier or more pronounced partial liquefaction and morphological changes than uniformly distributed controls at the same temperature.
Particles with minimal surface compositional variation retain an intact surface structure to higher temperatures.
Particles with minimal surface compositional variation have higher premelting onset temperatures than surface-enriched particles.
The proposed relationship applies mainly to 5–100 nm HEA nanoparticles whose compositional inhomogeneity favors differential surface mobility.
Particles outside the 5–100 nm range or with negligible surface segregation may not show early-onset premelting.
Substrate interactions may alter or overshadow the proposed surface-driven premelting behavior.
Equivalent premelting onset and morphological evolution in surface-enriched and uniform controls would falsify surface segregation as the primary driver.
